claim: Spatial frequency (SF) selectivity is a fundamental feature encoded in the visual system.
source: Spatial frequency (SF) selectivity is a fundamental feature encoded in the visual system.
evidence: This is a general statement about SF selectivity being fundamental, supported by the context of the manuscript and established scientific knowledge.

claim: The organization of SF selectivity is related to orientation and color maps in the primary visual cortex (V1) and have a high degree of periodicity in both cats and monkeys.
source: Previous studies have shown that the organization of SF selectivity is related to orientation and color maps in the primary visual cortex (V1) and have a high degree of periodicity in both cats (Hübener et al., 1997; Issa et al., 2000; Shoham et al., 1997; Tootell et al., 1981) and monkeys (Silverman et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Studies have consistently shown an orthogonal mapping of SF and orientation.
source: Studies have consistently shown an orthogonal mapping of SF and orientation, suggesting an efficient arrangement that provides each orientation access to a wide range of SFs (Issa et al., 2000; Nauhaus et al., 2012; Nauhaus et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Color representation in V1 is generally associated with a range of lower SFs.
source: In contrast, color representation in V1 (the color is represented in patches commonly referred to as 'blobs' in V1) is generally associated with a range of lower SFs (Silverman et al., 1989; Tootell et al., 1988).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: There is a gradient from high to low of SF representation across eccentricities.
source: Thus, in addition to a gradient from high to low of SF representation across eccentricities (Foster et al., 1985; De Valois et al., 1982; Lu et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2010), SF organization is further specified within local distinct functional regions.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The traditional view of the V2 hypercolumn comprises the alternating thin-pale-thick-pale stripe cycle.
source: The traditional view of the V2 hypercolumn comprises the alternating thin-pale-thick-pale stripe cycle (Horton, 1984; Livingstone and Hubel, 1984; Roe and Ts'o, 1995; Tootell et al., 1983).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Within thin stripes, surface properties, typically associated with low SF preferences, such as hue maps, 'brightness' maps, and ON/FF maps are represented.
source: Within thin stripes, surface properties, typically associated with low SF preferences, such as hue maps (Xiao et al., 2003), 'brightness' maps (Roe et al., 2005), and ON/FF maps (Wang et al., 2007) are represented.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Within the thick and pale stripes are higher-order orientation maps such as those defined by illusory contours, motion direction maps, and maps for motion-defined edges, as well as stereo-defined near-to-far disparity maps.
source: Within the thick and pale stripes are higher-order orientation maps such as those defined by illusory contours (Ramsden et al., 2001), motion direction maps (Lu et al., 2010), and maps for motion-defined edges (Chen et al., 2016), as well as stereo-defined near-to-far disparity maps (Chen et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: There is little systematic data relating SF representation in V2 to functional stripes.
source: There is little systematic data relating SF representation in V2 to functional stripes (cf., Gegenfurtner et al., 1996; Levitt et al., 1994; Tootell and Hamilton, 1989) and, despite previous attempts, few studies have demonstrated functional mapping of stripes based on SF alone (Lu and Roe, 2007; Lu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research and acknowledgment of gaps in the literature.

claim: In V4, surface and shape information are organized into 'color' and 'orientation' bands.
source: In V4, surface and shape information are organized into, for lack of better terminology, 'color' and 'orientation' bands.
evidence: This is a statement about V4 organization, supported by the context of the manuscript.

claim: Within the color bands, maps for hue and for luminance have been described.
source: Within the color bands, maps for hue and for luminance have been described (Tanigawa et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2020; Li et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Within orientation bands, there are maps for contrast-defined contours, disparity-defined contours, as well as maps for curvature degree and curvature orientation.
source: Within orientation bands, there are maps for contrast-defined contours (Hu et al., 2020; Li et al., 2013; Lu et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2020; Tanigawa et al., 2010), disparity-defined contours (Fang et al., 2019), as well as maps for curvature degree and curvature orientation (Hu et al., 2020; Ponce et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: How SF preference maps relate to other feature maps in V4 remains unknown.
source: Despite our growing understanding of functional organization in V4, how SF preference maps (first reported in Lu et al., 2018) relate to other feature maps in V4 remains unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about gaps in knowledge, supported by the context of the manuscript.

claim: Most of the imaged V1 region favored high SF stimuli, while most of the imaged V4 region favored low SF stimuli.
source: We found that in both cases, most of the imaged V1 region favored high SF stimuli, while most of the imaged V4 region favored low SF stimuli.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: For V1, the coverage ratio peaks at high SF, while for V4, the coverage ratio peaks at low SF.
source: For V1, the coverage ratio peaks at high SF (light gray bars in Figure 3C and G), while for V4, the coverage ratio peaks at low SF (black bars in Figure 3C and G), consistent with previous findings that V4 prefers lower SF than V1 (Lu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript and figures, and is consistent with previous findings.

claim: The preferred SFs significantly decrease from V1 to V4.
source: The preferred SFs (Figure 3D and H) significantly decrease from V1 to V4 (see Table 1, Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, V1 vs. V4, V2 vs. V4, V1 vs. V2, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript and figures, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Gratings with low SFs evoked clear selective responses in all imaged V4 regions, whereas gratings with high SFs only evoked responses in certain regions, mostly in the lateral part of the cortex.
source: We found that the functional map at a specific SF is not always easily ascertained. Gratings with low SFs (e.g., 0.25 cycles/deg, 0.5 cycles/deg) evoked clear selective responses (Figure 4D, thresholded, right panel) in all imaged V4 regions, whereas gratings with high SFs only evoked responses in certain regions, mostly in the lateral part of the cortex (toward foveal representation, red star).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: As SF increases, the location of the selective activation center shifts from medial to lateral across the cortex.
source: As SF increases, the location of the selective activation center shifts from medial to lateral across the cortex (Figure 4C, blue dots).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: The activation center of color-selective response shifted from medial to lateral with increasing SF.
source: Thus, the activation center of color-selective response also shifted from medial to lateral with increasing SF (Figure 4C, orange dots).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: When only a few SFs are tested, the coverage ratio of the orientation and color domains is underestimated.
source: We found that, when only a few SFs are tested, the coverage ratio of the orientation and color domains is underestimated (see white numbers in upper corners in Figure 4A, B, D and E), underscoring the importance of testing a wide range of SFs.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: Orientation domains and color domains tend to separate in space, forming different functional bands.
source: As reported in previous V4 studies (Tanigawa et al., 2010; Li et al., 2013), orientation domains and color domains tend to separate in space, forming different functional bands.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: For the lateral orientation and color bands, the percentage values were higher for high SFs.
source: We found that for the lateral orientation and color bands (see the two bands < 6 mm), the percentage values were higher for high SFs (blue/cyan lines vs. red/orange lines).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: For the medial orientation and color bands, the percentage values were higher for low SFs.
source: In comparison, for the medial orientation and color bands (see the two bands >6 mm), the percentage values were higher for low SFs (red/orange lines vs. blue/cyan lines).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The proportions of activated pixels in color and orientation domains in the lateral and medial parts of V4 change with SFs in distinct ways.
source: We found that the proportions of activated pixels in color and orientation domains in the lateral and medial parts of V4 change with SFs in distinct ways.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In parafoveal cortex (medial), for both orientation and color domains, the proportion of pixels tends to decrease with increasing SF.
source: In parafoveal cortex (medial), for both orientation and color domains, the proportion of pixels tends to decrease with increasing SF; in foveal cortex (lateral), for both orientation and color domains, the proportion of pixels increase as SF increases.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In foveal cortex (lateral), for both orientation and color domains, the proportion of pixels increase as SF increases.
source: In parafoveal cortex (medial), for both orientation and color domains, the proportion of pixels tends to decrease with increasing SF; in foveal cortex (lateral), for both orientation and color domains, the proportion of pixels increase as SF increases.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The exposed areas of V1 are in the lateral region of the hemisphere, corresponding to the eccentricity of 0–2°.
source: The exposed areas of V1 are in the lateral region of the hemisphere, corresponding to the eccentricity of 0–2°; here low SFs barely evoke measurable selective orientation responses (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, left column, cases 1–3).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: The orientation map in the lateral region is only apparent at high SFs.
source: The orientation map in the lateral region is only apparent at high SFs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, >1 cycle/deg).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: For both V1 and V4, the selective activation center moves from medial to lateral as SF increases.
source: Although the optimal SF differs between V1 and V4, for both areas, the selective activation center moves from medial to lateral as SF increases (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, cases 1–4, dots of different shading correspond to the activation centers at different SFs).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: The foveal regions of V1, V2, and V4 are located in the lateral part of the cortex.
source: In monkey visual cortex, the foveal regions of V1, V2, and V4 are located in the lateral part of the cortex (Gattass et al., 1981; Gattass et al., 1988 see Figure 2D), in agreement with the findings from electrophysiology studies that foveal regions favor high SF (Perry and Cowey, 1985; Schein, 1988; Wässle et al., 1989; Wilder et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: For orientation maps, high correlation values appeared in the comparisons among high SF conditions in foveal region.
source: For orientation maps (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A), high correlation values (>0.5) appeared in the comparisons among high SF conditions in foveal region.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: For orientation maps, high correlation values appeared in the comparisons among low SF conditions in parafoveal region.
source: In contrast, high correlation values appeared in the comparisons among low SF conditions in parafoveal region.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: For color functional maps, higher correlation values were measured under low SF conditions in both foveal and parafoveal regions.
source: For color functional maps (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B), higher correlation values were measured under low SF conditions in both foveal and parafoveal regions, while high correlation values appeared only in the foveal region under high SF conditions.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: Independent of the type of visual information presented (orientation or color), parafoveal regions tend to process the visual input containing relatively low SF components, while visual input containing high SF components is better processed in foveal regions.
source: These differences reflect distinct capabilities of different cortical regions (fovea vs. parafovea). Independent of the type of visual information presented (orientation or color), parafoveal regions tend to process the visual input containing relatively low SF components, while visual input containing high SF components is better processed in foveal regions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In V4, the foveal region is capable of processing visual information with a broad range of SF sensitivity.
source: In V4, the foveal region is capable of processing visual information with a broad range of SF sensitivity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In V2 and V4, the iso-orientation and iso-SF contours that intersected at large angles were found most frequently.
source: In V2 and V4, the iso-orientation and iso-SF contours that intersected at large angles were found most frequently (see Figure 6G, K and O, Figure 6—figure supplement 2G and K).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: There are more 60–90° intersection angles than other kinds of intersection angles in the orientation-selective regions.
source: The results indicate that there are more (percentage value) 60–90° intersection angles than other kinds of intersection angles in the orientation-selective regions (see white patches in Figure 6F, J and N).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: The percentage of the large angle group is significantly higher than the small and medium groups.
source: The percentage of the large angle group is significantly higher than the small (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p=1.60 × 10–5, n = 15 from five regions, two V2 regions, and three V4 regions) and medium groups (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p=1.73 × 10–4).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The percentage difference in large intersection angle (60–90°) is significant between groups with strong orientation selectivity and weak orientation selectivity.
source: The percentage difference in large intersection angle (60–90°) is also significant (strong orientation selectivity group, n = 15 from five regions, two V2 regions, and three V4 regions; weak orientation selectivity group, labeled as '60–90° Ref.' in Figure 6V, n = 6 from two V4 regions; Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p=0.0057, see Figure 6V).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript and figures, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Low SF preference domains tend to co-localize with V4 color domains to a greater extent than high SF preference domains.
source: In this case, low SF preference domains tend to co-localize with V4 color domains to a greater extent than high SF preference domains (21.3% vs 8.3% of all pixels in color domains).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The total amount of cortex able to discriminate high SF vs. low SF is only a small portion of the total V4 area.
source: In these four cases, we found that the total amount of cortex able to discriminate high SF vs. low SF (high SF plus low SF pixels) is only a small portion of the total V4 area (coverage ratio of high SF preference domains in V4: 3.9% ± 1.5%, mean ± SD; coverage ratio of low SF preference domains in V4: 6.0% ± 3.7%, mean ± SD.; coverage ratio: the area of SF domains divided by the imaged area of V4).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In all cases, there is a great tendency for low SF domains to overlap with color domains.
source: Although the difference is not statistically significant (four cases, Wilcoxon test, p>0.05), in all cases, we found a great tendency for low SF domains to overlap with color domains (the percentage of high SF preference regions in color domains: 3.9% ± 3.3%; the percentage of low SF preference regions in color domains: 13.3% ± 8.4%, Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: The SF preference changed across V2.
source: We hypothesize that this controversy is due to the inability of cytochrome oxidase staining to reliably identify stripe type, which functional imaging can securely address. To further explore this, we first examined whether there were measurable SF preference differences in V2. As indicated in the map, the SF preference changed across V2 (same as V2 in Figure 3B, the region between lunate sulcus and V1/V2 border indicated by red arrow).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: The low SF preference regions are well correlated with color preference domains.
source: The low SF preference regions obtained using these two methods (white patches, in the differential SF map, see Figure 7F; red/orange regions, in the colored SF preference map, see Figure 7I and J) are well correlated with color preference domains (red dashed circles in Figure 7F and black patches in Figure 7G and H).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: For subtraction between high SF and low SF conditions, high SF preference domains can be detected in the foveal region.
source: For subtraction between high SF (>1 cycle/deg) and low SF (0.5 cycles/deg) conditions, high SF preference domains can be detected in the foveal region (red star, see black patches indicated by red arrows in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: For the subtraction between medium SF and low SF conditions, the relatively high SF preference domains can only be detected in the parafoveal region.
source: However, for the subtraction between medium SF (1 cycle/deg) and low SF (0.25 cycles/deg) conditions, the relatively high SF preference domains can only be detected in the parafoveal region (see black patches indicated by blue arrows in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: From parafoveal to foveal region, the preferred SF tends to increase gradually.
source: These results indicate from parafoveal to foveal region, the preferred SF tends to increase gradually.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Both SF preference and color selectivity vary along the V1/V2 border.
source: Both SF preference (red lines) and color selectivity (black lines) vary along the V1/V2 border (Figure 7G–L).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: Color selectivity was found in or near low SF preference regions.
source: Color selectivity was found in or near low SF preference regions (see also Figure 7F, red dashed circles and white patches in V2); however, not all low SF preference regions exhibited strong color selectivity.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: SF preference differences vary uniquely within V2.
source: Thus, SF preference differences vary uniquely within V2 (see Figure 7M).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: The differences in SF preference between the regions on the two sides of a thin stripe may correlate to the reported two types (medial vs. lateral) of pale stripes in V2.
source: The differences in SF preference between the regions on the two sides of a thin stripe (see Figure 7K and L, thin stripe location: around the peaks of the black lines) may correlate to the reported two types (medial vs. lateral) of pale stripes in V2 (Felleman et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the experimental data and previous research.

claim: With respect to topography, the SF population response of V4 orientation and color domains shift systematically with topographic location.
source: We found (1) Topography: With respect to topography, the SF population response of V4 orientation and color domains shift systematically with topographic location.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The geometric centroids of the selective response shift toward foveolar (lateral) parts of the cortex as SF increases.
source: To be specific, the geometric centroids of the selective response shift toward foveolar (lateral) parts of the cortex as SF increases.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The foveal region of V4 was responsive to a broad range of SF from high to low, suggesting greater SF integration at higher cortical levels, even in foveal regions.
source: Interestingly, distinct from V1 fovea, which was selectively responsive to orientations of higher SFs (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), the foveal region of V4 was responsive to a broad range of SF from high to low, suggesting greater SF integration at higher cortical levels, even in foveal regions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: Within V4 and V2, similar to what was previously shown in V1, the gradients of orientation and SF maps tend to be orthogonal to one another.
source: (2) Orthogonal primary axes: Within V4 and V2, similar to what was previously shown in V1, the gradients of orientation and SF maps tend to be orthogonal to one another.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: There is a tendency for low SF preference domains to overlap with color domains in V4 and V2.
source: (3) Low SF bias in V4 and V2 color domains: We find there is a tendency for low SF preference domains to overlap with color domains in V4 and V2.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Orthogonal crossings between different cortical maps facilitate the maximum combination of response properties in a local area with columnar organization.
source: As mentioned in many previous studies, orthogonal crossings between different cortical maps facilitate the maximum combination of response properties in a local area with columnar organization.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: This kind of spatial relationship has now been reported in different animals (cat, monkey) and between different functional maps including orientation vs. ocular dominance, orientation vs. SF in cat area 17; orientation vs. ocular dominance, orientation vs. SF in monkey V1; hue vs. lightness in macaque V1; orientation vs. disparity in macaque V2 and, in this study, orientation vs. SF in macaque V2 and V4.
source: This kind of spatial relationship has now been reported in different animals (cat, monkey) and between different functional maps including orientation vs. ocular dominance, orientation vs. SF in cat area 17 (Hübener et al., 1997); orientation vs. ocular dominance, orientation vs. SF in monkey V1 (Bartfeld and Grinvald, 1992; Nauhaus et al., 2012; Obermayer and Blasdel, 1993); hue vs. lightness in macaque V1 (Li et al., 2022); orientation vs. disparity in macaque V2 (Chen et al., 2008; Ts'o et al., 2009) and, in this study, orientation vs. SF in macaque V2 and V4.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research and the current study.

claim: This orthogonality may be a common principle and reveals key parameters specific to each cortical area.
source: We suggest that this orthogonality may be a common principle and reveals key parameters specific to each cortical area.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the experimental data and previous research.

claim: For object structure, orientation and SF are two key parameters; for color, the key parameters are hue and luminance.
source: Thus, for object structure, orientation and SF are two key parameters; for color, the key parameters are hue and luminance (Li et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the experimental data and previous research.

claim: These combinations ensure a complete representation of basic shape and surface information at each cortical level.
source: These combinations ensure a complete representation of basic shape and surface information at each cortical level.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the experimental data.

claim: Cortical mosaics contain distinct regions of orthogonal feature parameters, as observed in the color and orientation stripes of V2 and the color and orientation bands of V4, and may present for other parameters (e.g., face space, object space) in higher cortical areas.
source: Thus, cortical mosaics contain distinct regions of orthogonal feature parameters, as observed in the color and orientation stripes of V2 and the color and orientation bands of V4, and may present for other parameters (e.g., face space, object space) in higher cortical areas.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the experimental data.

claim: The majority of V4 regions favor low SF relative to V1.
source: Consistent with previous findings (Desimone and Schein, 1987; Lu et al., 2018), our results indicate that the majority of V4 regions favor low SF relative to V1 (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript and figures, consistent with previous findings.

claim: For both V4 orientation- and color-selective response, there is a tendency for representation to shift to higher SFs from parafovea to fovea.
source: For both V4 orientation- and color-selective response, there is a tendency for representation to shift to higher SFs from parafovea to fovea (Figure 4 with three supplements, and Figure 5 with one supplement), supporting the inverse relationship between SF preference and retinal eccentricity (Desimone and Schein, 1987; Lu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript and figures, supporting previous findings.

claim: In foveal V4 region, even at low SF, robust orientation- and color-selective responses are detected.
source: However, it should be noted that in foveal V4 region, even at low SF, robust orientation- and color-selective responses are detected.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Foveal representation in V4 may be better organized for processing complex images (e.g., natural scenes) with multiple SF components.
source: This points to an important difference between V1 and V4. That is, foveal representation in V4 may be better organized for processing complex images (e.g., natural scenes) with multiple SF components.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the experimental data.

claim: SF preference changes within the exposed V2 area, forming different SF preference patches.
source: We found that similar to color-selective response, SF preference changes within the exposed V2 area, forming different SF preference patches, which supports a general functional layout for SF coding in the visual system (preference for low SF in V1 blob, V2/V4 low SF domains; preference for high SF in V1 interblob, V2/V4 high SF domains).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In elongated cortical areas such as V2 there tend to be periodic changes in response features across the cortical surface.
source: As suggested by modeling V2 retinotopic maps of tree shrews (Sedigh-Sarvestani et al., 2021), in elongated cortical areas such as V2 there tend to be periodic changes in response features across the cortical surface.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: A putative functional implication of this periodic distribution is to aid in the integration across features spaces (wiring minimization) via horizontal connections in V2.
source: Another putative functional implication of this periodic distribution is to aid in the integration across features spaces (wiring minimization) via horizontal connections in V2 (Chklovskii et al., 2002; Cowey, 1979; Hubel and Wiesel, 1977; Mitchison, 1991; Koulakov and Chklovskii, 2001).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to previous research.

claim: At the scale of visual field representation, there is a broad and downward shifting range of SFs from center to periphery.
source: At the scale of visual field representation, there is a broad and downward shifting range of SFs from center to periphery.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Within this global SF map lie hypercolumns of repeated orientation and color representation, each of which contains two orthogonally arranged primary parameters.
source: Within this global SF map lie hypercolumns of repeated orientation and color representation, each of which contains two orthogonally arranged primary parameters.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: In the 'orientation' regions, SF is systematically and orthogonally mapped in relation to the orientation map.
source: In the 'orientation' regions, SF is systematically and orthogonally mapped in relation to the orientation map (this study); in the 'color' regions, hue and lightness are orthogonally mapped (Li et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings presented in the manuscript and previous research.

claim: In the 'color' regions, hue and lightness are orthogonally mapped.
source: In the 'orientation' regions, SF is systematically and orthogonally mapped in relation to the orientation map (this study); in the 'color' regions, hue and lightness are orthogonally mapped (Li et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The primary parameter spaces mapped in each cortical area change from one area to another.
source: Analogous to how the primary parameter spaces mapped in each cortical area change from one area to another (e.g., V1: ocular dominance, orientation, color; V2: higher-order orientation, hue, disparity; V4: curvature, 3D shape from shading, hue and lightness, Hu et al., 2020; Srinath et al., 2021; face areas: face maps, Kanwisher et al., 1997, Chang and Tsao, 2017; object areas: object maps, Bao et al., 2020), we hypothesize that subregions of a cortical hypercolumn also organize for different parameters.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Subregions of a cortical hypercolumn also organize for different parameters.
source: Analogous to how the primary parameter spaces mapped in each cortical area change from one area to another (e.g., V1: ocular dominance, orientation, color; V2: higher-order orientation, hue, disparity; V4: curvature, 3D shape from shading, hue and lightness, Hu et al., 2020; Srinath et al., 2021; face areas: face maps, Kanwisher et al., 1997, Chang and Tsao, 2017; object areas: object maps, Bao et al., 2020), we hypothesize that subregions of a cortical hypercolumn also organize for different parameters.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the experimental data and previous research.

claim: While SF is an important primary axis in orientation regions, in color regions which by nature are associated with low SFs, the rationale for a systematic SF map is weakened.
source: Thus, while SF is an important primary axis in orientation regions, in color regions which by nature are associated with low SFs, the rationale for a systematic SF map is weakened.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the experimental data.

claim: One could view the color regions as evolutionary 'add-ons,' which became tacked on to the low end of the SF continuum.
source: One could view the color regions as evolutionary 'add-ons,' which became tacked on to the low end of the SF continuum.
evidence: This is a speculative statement.

claim: The functional maps or regions (e.g., orientation, color) in V2 and V4 are not simple repeats of the functional representation in V1, although here they have the same name (orientation, color).
source: It should be noted that the functional maps or regions (e.g., orientation, color) in V2 and V4 are not simple repeats of the functional representation in V1, although here they have the same name (orientation, color).
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: These maps or regions are dedicated to processing different visual information in different visual areas.
source: These maps or regions are dedicated to processing different visual information in different visual areas.
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: The architecture of SF representation, which describes distinct SF representations within orientation and color regions, further extends and supports the view of continued parallel streaming of feature-specific pathways.
source: We suggest the architecture of SF representation, which describes distinct SF representations within orientation and color regions, further extends and supports the view of continued parallel streaming of feature-specific pathways.
